title: The aid system is doing less with less, yet grading itself far too kindly
gist: McGlasson and Maung argue ALNAP's 2022-25 State of the Humanitarian System report shows aid reaching fewer people with less (funding per targeted person halved to US$90 in 2025 versus US$255 need), while the system rebrands shrinkage as efficiency. They urge donors to channel a rising share directly to local responders, who form 81% of organisations but got 4.3% of direct funding in 2025.

insights.claim: For eight months not one minimum humanitarian standard was met for the 600,000 people displaced in Goma, eastern DRC, according to the humanitarian system's own report card.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Signals severe unmet need and instability risk in eastern DRC, a key minerals region.

insights.claim: Funding per targeted person halved from US$178 in 2021 to US$90 in 2025 while the estimated cost of meeting each person's needs rose to around US$255.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Widening humanitarian funding gap raises odds of instability and displacement in crisis zones.
insights.quote: funding for each person targeted halved from US$178 in 2021 to US$90 in 2025, while the estimated cost of meeting each person’s needs rose to around US$255

insights.claim: More than 90% of World Food Program in-kind rations in 2023 failed to meet nutritional needs, and about 80% were still inadequate in 2024.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Food aid inadequacy compounds famine and migration risks.

insights.claim: With USAID dismantled and other donors cutting deeply, the next reporting cycle will almost certainly look worse.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Aid retrenchment is a durable trend, increasing fragility in aid-dependent states.
insights.quote: With USAID dismantled and other donors cutting deeply, the next reporting cycle will almost certainly look worse.

insights.claim: The humanitarian system is failing more cheaply, not more efficiently, rebranding shrinkage as efficiency at the expense of people in crisis and local responders.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Be sceptical of efficiency claims from aid agencies facing budget cuts.
insights.quote: It is simply failing more cheaply.

insights.claim: ALNAP's authors concede that without strong cost and outcome data there is no way to tell whether lower spending reflects efficiency gains or less adequate assistance.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Efficiency is unverified, undermining donor justifications for cuts.

insights.claim: The UN's 2026 appeals were billed as 'hyper-prioritised', using a narrower definition of need that made the shortfall look smaller while many in need went uncounted.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Headline appeal gaps understate true humanitarian need.

insights.claim: Cash and flexible multiyear funding are proven to deliver better value, yet the share of UN agencies and international NGOs giving multiyear funding to partners fell.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Cost-cutting is perversely eroding the most efficient delivery modalities.

insights.claim: In 2025, 67% of practitioners rated their targeting good or excellent, but only 51% of recipients agreed and just 53% said aid met their most important needs.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson

insights.claim: Local and national groups make up 81% of humanitarian organisations and 94% of staff are nationals, yet in 2025 local actors received only 4.3% of funding directly and national NGOs held 11% of Humanitarian Country Team seats.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Cost savings are shifted onto under-resourced local actors.
insights.quote: Yet in 2025, local actors received just 4.3% of humanitarian funding directly

insights.claim: In Sudan, more than 600 community-run Emergency Response Rooms, rooted in the nafeer mutual-aid tradition and largely diaspora-funded, have become the central relief network.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Diaspora remittance-funded networks are a key channel for relief in Sudan.

insights.claim: A Deakin University report found funders focused more on managing perceived risk than community needs, and the number of Sudanese organisations funded by major donors fell sharply.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Donor risk-aversion is starving effective local delivery.

insights.claim: Donors should channel a fixed and rising share of humanitarian funding directly to local responders, using pooled funds and accountable intermediaries where direct transfers are impossible.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Shift could reshape humanitarian funding flows away from international agencies.

insights.claim: Multiyear, ideally cash-based, funding should be the default in protracted crises, and local responders need real decision-making power, not just more budget.
insights.speaker: Mary Ana McGlasson
insights.so_what: Cash-based aid growth benefits digital payment and remittance rails in crisis zones.
